points.guide: A uniform magnetic field induces an emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicularly to it as given by $\varepsilon = BvL$. (Guidance: relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field.)
aims: Explain why an emf is induced in a straight conductor moving through a magnetic field.
Derive and use $\varepsilon = BvL$ for a conductor moving at right angles to a uniform field.

slides.title: Charges on the move
bullets: A charge at rest in a magnetic field feels no magnetic force
A charge moving at speed $v$ at right angles to a field $B$ feels a force $qvB$ (D.3)
A metal rod is full of free electrons: move the rod and they move with it
So moving the rod through a field pushes its free electrons along the rod
One end becomes negative and the other positive: an induced emf appears between the ends
slides.notes: Use the right-hand rule from D.3 for a positive charge; the electrons drift the opposite way. Quick demonstration: move a wire between the poles of a horseshoe magnet with a sensitive centre-zero meter connected.

slides.title: Relative motion is what matters
bullets: Push a magnet into a coil joined to a meter: the needle moves only while the magnet moves
Pull it out again: the deflection reverses
Hold the magnet still and move the coil instead: the same readings
Move faster: a bigger deflection
An emf is induced whenever a conductor and a magnetic field move relative to each other
slides.notes: Ask for predictions before each step. Faraday first saw induction in 1831 as a brief flick of a galvanometer needle, so this is a good moment for the Nature of science point about careful observation.

slides.title: Deriving ε = BvL
slides.start: Take a straight conductor of length $L$ travelling at speed $v$, perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. Its free charges move with it, so each one feels a magnetic force along the conductor.

steps.text: The magnetic force on each free charge
Charge piles up at the ends, making an electric field along the conductor
The electric force on each charge
Charges stop drifting when the two forces balance

slides.notes: Step 2 uses $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$ for a uniform field (D.2). The same result comes from Faraday's law later in the lesson.

slides.title: Emf in a moving conductor
bullets: $L$ is the length of the conductor inside the field
The conductor, its velocity and the field are all at right angles
Twice the speed gives twice the emf

slides.title: Tips for using ε = BvL
bullets: Use only the length of conductor that is inside the field
Use the field component at right angles to both the conductor and its velocity
An aircraft wing moving horizontally cuts only the vertical component of the Earth's field
Convert µT and mT to T, and cm to m, before you substitute
An emf appears even in an open circuit; a current flows only if the circuit is complete

slides.title: A car aerial
slides.question: A car drives due east at 30 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Its radio aerial is a straight vertical metal rod 0.80 m long. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field there is 20 µT, pointing north. Find the emf induced between the ends of the aerial.
slides.hint: Check that the aerial, its velocity and this field component are all at right angles to each other, then use $\varepsilon = BvL$. Convert µT to T first.

steps.text: Vertical rod, moving east, field pointing north: all at right angles
The emf is less than a millivolt

slides.notes: The vertical component of the field would push charges sideways across the rod, not along it, so it adds nothing to the emf between the ends.

slides.title: Finding the speed
slides.question: In a demonstration, a copper rod 0.15 m long is moved at right angles to a uniform field of 0.060 T between two large magnets. A voltmeter connected across the ends of the rod by long flexible leads reads 6.3 mV. Find the speed of the rod.
slides.hint: Rearrange $\varepsilon = BvL$ to make $v$ the subject, and write the emf in volts.
slides.notes: The leads stay still while the rod moves, so they do not have the same emf induced in them.

points.guide: Magnetic flux $\Phi$ as given by $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$.
aims: Calculate magnetic flux using $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ measured from the normal to the area.
Calculate the flux linkage $N\Phi$ of a coil of $N$ turns.

slides.title: Field through an area
bullets: The emf a loop gets depends on how much field passes through it
Field parallel to the plane of the loop: no field lines cross it
Field at right angles to the plane: the most field lines cross it
Describe the loop's direction by its normal, the line at right angles to its plane
Magnetic flux $\Phi$ measures how much field passes through an area
slides.notes: Hold up a hoop in front of a row of parallel metre rules (the field lines) and tilt it: students can count how many rules pass through it.

slides.title: Magnetic flux
bullets: $\theta$ is the angle between $B$ and the normal to the area
Unit: the weber, $1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T m}^{2}$
Largest when $\theta = 0$; zero when $\theta = 90^\circ$

slides.title: Flux density and flux linkage
bullets: With the field at right angles to the area, $B = \dfrac{\Phi}{A}$: so $B$ is also called the magnetic flux density
Flux can be negative: turning a loop over, from $\theta = 0$ to $180^\circ$, reverses its sign
In a coil of $N$ turns, the same flux passes through every turn
Flux linkage $= N\Phi$, also measured in Wb
slides.notes: Some books write the unit of flux linkage as Wb-turns. Either is accepted.

slides.title: Measuring θ from the normal
bullets: $\theta$ is between $B$ and the normal, not between $B$ and the loop
If you are given the angle to the plane, the angle to the normal is $90^\circ$ minus it

slides.title: Tips for flux calculations
bullets: Check which angle you are given: to the normal, or to the plane?
If the angle $\alpha$ is to the plane, then $\Phi = BA\sin\alpha$
Circle: $A = \pi r^{2}$; rectangle: length × width
Flux has no $N$ in it; flux linkage does

slides.title: A loop at three angles
slides.question: A square wire loop of side 12 cm is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.35 T. Find the flux through the loop when the normal to the loop is at (a) $0^\circ$, (b) $50^\circ$ and (c) $90^\circ$ to the field.
slides.hint: Find the area in $\text{m}^{2}$ first, then use $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ three times.

steps.text: (c) $\cos 90^\circ = 0$: the field runs along the plane of the loop

slides.title: Angle to the plane
slides.question: A 150-turn rectangular coil measures 8.0 cm by 5.0 cm. A uniform field of 0.20 T makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the plane of the coil. Find (a) the flux through one turn and (b) the flux linkage of the coil.
slides.hint: The angle given is to the plane, not to the normal. What is the angle between the field and the normal?

steps.text: Angle between the field and the normal
(b) Multiply by the number of turns

slides.notes: Using $\cos 30^\circ$ by mistake gives $6.9 \times 10^{-4}$ Wb: a favourite trap in exam questions.

points.guide: A time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf $\varepsilon$ as given by Faraday's law of induction $\varepsilon = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. (Guidance: time-varying magnetic fields; a magnet oscillating on a spring above a conducting coil.)
aims: State Faraday's law and use $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ to calculate induced emfs.
Describe how a time-varying field or a magnet oscillating near a coil changes the flux linkage and induces an emf.

slides.title: Only a changing flux induces an emf
bullets: A steady flux, however large, induces nothing
Since $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, the flux changes when:
$B$ changes: a magnet moves, or a nearby current switches on or off
the area $A$ inside the field changes: a coil moves into or out of a field
the angle $\theta$ changes: a coil rotates
A faster change gives a bigger emf

slides.title: Two coils, no connection
bullets: Coil 1 is joined to a cell and a switch; coil 2, close by, only to a meter
Close the switch: the meter kicks once, then returns to zero
While the current is steady: no reading at all
Open the switch: a kick the other way
The growing or collapsing field of coil 1 changes the flux through coil 2
Transformers and wireless phone chargers use this idea
slides.notes: This is close to the experiment Faraday did in 1831, with two coils wound on an iron ring. Winding both coils on one iron core makes the kicks much bigger.

slides.title: Two coils on one iron core
slides.alt: An iron ring with two coils wound on opposite sides. Coil 1 is joined to a cell and a switch. Coil 2 is joined only to a meter, G.
bullets: Coil 1: a cell and a switch. Coil 2: only a meter
The iron core carries coil 1's flux through coil 2
The meter kicks only while the switch closes or opens

slides.title: Faraday's law
bullets: The size of the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage
$N\Delta\Phi$ is the change in flux linkage in a time $\Delta t$
The minus sign is Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change

slides.title: ε = BvL from Faraday's law
slides.start: A rod of length $L$ slides at speed $v$ along two rails joined by a resistor, so rod, rails and resistor make a circuit. A uniform field $B$ is at right angles to the plane of the circuit.

steps.text: In a time $\Delta t$ the rod moves a distance
The area of the circuit grows by
So the flux through the circuit grows by
Faraday's law for one turn, size only

slides.notes: Two pictures, one result: the force on the moving charges, and the changing flux through the circuit.

slides.title: A magnet on a spring
bullets: A magnet bounces on a spring above a coil joined to a data logger
As the magnet moves, the flux linkage of the coil rises and falls
The emf is largest near the middle of the motion, where the magnet moves fastest
The emf is zero at the top and the bottom, where the magnet is momentarily at rest
The emf alternates: its sign changes each time the magnet changes direction
If a current flows, it takes energy from the magnet, so the oscillation dies away faster
slides.notes: Data loggers show this well. Let students sketch the emf–time graph before you show it.

slides.title: The emf from a bouncing magnet
slides.alt: Left: a bar magnet hangs on a spring above a coil joined to a data logger, and moves up and down. Right: graphs against time of the magnet's height, a dashed cosine curve, and the induced emf, a sine curve a quarter of a cycle out of step. The emf is zero when the magnet is at the top or the bottom.
bullets: The emf is zero at the top and the bottom, where the magnet stops
It is greatest as the magnet passes the middle, moving fastest
So the emf is a quarter of a cycle out of step with the height
slides.notes: Drawn without damping, for small oscillations. A real trace is not a perfect sine curve, and the sign of the emf depends on how the coil is connected.

slides.title: Tips for Faraday's law
bullets: It is the rate of change of the flux that matters, not its size
Find $\Delta\Phi$ first: $\Delta B \times A$, or $B \times \Delta A$, or a change in $\cos\theta$
Turning a coil over changes its flux from $+BA$ to $-BA$, so $\Delta\Phi = 2BA$
On a graph of $N\Phi$ against $t$, the emf is minus the gradient
Leave out the minus sign when only the size is asked for, and use Lenz's law for the direction
If the rate of change is not steady, $N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ gives the average emf

slides.title: Switching on an electromagnet
slides.question: A 120-turn coil of area $3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{2}$ sits between the poles of an electromagnet, with its plane at right angles to the field. When the electromagnet is switched on, the field rises steadily from zero to 0.45 T in 0.15 s. Find the size of the emf induced in the coil.
slides.hint: Only $B$ changes, so find $\Delta\Phi = \Delta B \times A$ for one turn, then use Faraday's law.

steps.text: Change in flux through one turn

slides.notes: Once the field is steady, the emf drops to zero, even though the flux is now at its largest.

slides.title: Turning a coil over in the Earth's field
slides.question: A flat coil of 500 turns, each of area $1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^{2}$, is held with its normal along the Earth's magnetic field, of strength 50 µT. It is turned over through $180^\circ$ in 0.10 s. Find the average emf induced in the coil.
slides.hint: After half a turn, the same field passes through the coil the opposite way. What is the change in flux through one turn?

steps.text: Flux through one turn at the start

slides.notes: Students who use $\Delta\Phi = \Phi$ get half the answer. Coils like this were once used to measure the Earth's field.

points.guide: The direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz's law and is a consequence of energy conservation.
aims: Use Lenz's law to find the direction of an induced current.
Explain why Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy.

slides.title: Lenz's law
bullets: The induced emf, and any induced current, acts to oppose the change that produces it
This is the minus sign in Faraday's law
Push a north pole towards a coil: the near end of the coil becomes a north pole and repels it
Pull the north pole away: the near end becomes a south pole and attracts it back
The coil opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself

slides.title: Opposing the magnet
bullets: You have to do work to push the magnet in
That work becomes electrical energy in the circuit

slides.title: Why it must be so: energy
bullets: Imagine the induced current helped the change instead
The magnet would speed up, the current would grow, and so would the pull on the magnet
Kinetic and electrical energy would grow from nothing: impossible
So the induced current must oppose the change
The electrical energy always comes from work done against the opposing force
slides.notes: This is an argument by contradiction: assume the opposite and show that it breaks conservation of energy.

slides.title: Finding the direction
bullets: Is the flux through the circuit increasing or decreasing, and which way does it point?
The induced current makes its own field to oppose that change:
flux increasing: the induced field points the opposite way
flux decreasing: the induced field points the same way
Use the right-hand grip rule to turn that field direction into a current direction
In a broken circuit an emf is still induced, but no current flows, so there is no opposing force

slides.title: A rod on rails
bullets: Pulling the rod to the right increases the flux into the page
The induced current is anticlockwise: its field is out of the page inside the loop
The current in the rod feels a force $BIL$ that opposes the motion

slides.title: Electromagnetic braking
bullets: A strong magnet falls slowly down a copper pipe: currents induced in the pipe oppose its motion
Some trains, roller coasters and exercise bikes brake with magnets near metal discs or fins, without touching them
The kinetic energy becomes thermal energy in the metal
Slots cut in the metal break up the current loops and weaken the braking
slides.notes: Drop a neodymium magnet and a similar unmagnetised piece of metal down a copper pipe side by side. The concept challenge on the two hanging rings makes a good follow-up.

slides.title: A magnet in a copper pipe
slides.alt: A bar magnet, N pole down, falls inside a copper pipe. Induced current loops circle the pipe above and below the magnet. The loop above attracts the S pole; the loop below repels the N pole.
bullets: Below the magnet the flux is increasing: the induced current repels the N pole
Above it the flux is decreasing: the induced current attracts the S pole
Both forces act upwards, opposing the fall

slides.title: Self-induction
bullets: A changing current in a coil changes the flux through that same coil
So it induces an emf in the coil itself: self-induction
This back emf acts against the change in current: Lenz's law again
Switching on: the current rises gradually rather than instantly
Switching off a large coil suddenly: the emf can be big enough to make a spark jump across the switch
slides.notes: Required for exams in 2025–2027, qualitatively only (inductance and RL circuits are not required). Changed for exams from 2028: the 2028 guide no longer includes self-induction, so for those students this slide is background that helps with Lenz’s law.

slides.title: A magnet pulled away
slides.question: The south pole of a bar magnet is held close to one end of a coil joined to a meter. The magnet is then pulled quickly away from the coil, along its axis. State the magnetic pole induced at the near end of the coil, and explain whether the coil helps or hinders the movement.
slides.hint: Is the flux from the magnet through the coil increasing or decreasing? The coil acts to oppose that change.

steps.text: Moving the magnet away decreases the flux through the coil
To oppose the decrease, the coil pulls the magnet back: it attracts it
Unlike poles attract, so the near end of the coil becomes a north pole
The attraction hinders the movement: the work done pulling the magnet away becomes electrical energy

slides.title: A loop on the bench
slides.question: A rectangular wire loop lies flat on a bench. A uniform magnetic field passes vertically upwards through it, and the field is getting weaker. Viewed from above, is the induced current in the loop clockwise or anticlockwise?
slides.hint: Decide which way the loop's own field must point, inside the loop, to oppose the change. Then use the right-hand grip rule.

steps.text: The upward flux through the loop is decreasing
To oppose the decrease, the induced current makes an upward field inside the loop
Right-hand grip: with the thumb pointing up, the fingers curl anticlockwise seen from above
The induced current is anticlockwise, viewed from above

slides.notes: Ask what changes if the field is getting stronger instead (the current reverses), or if the loop is cut (no current, but still an emf).

points.guide: Guidance: a quantitative treatment of rectangular coils moving in and out of fields (for example, a coil moved in or out of the region of a magnetic field).
aims: Use $\varepsilon = NBvL$ for a rectangular coil moving into or out of a uniform field.
Sketch how the flux linkage and the emf change as a coil crosses a field region.

slides.title: A coil crossing a field
bullets: Entering: only the leading side cuts the field, so $\varepsilon = NBvL$
$L$ is the length of the side crossing the edge of the field
Fully inside a uniform field: the flux is constant, so $\varepsilon = 0$
Leaving: $\varepsilon = NBvL$ again, with the opposite sign
While a current flows in the coil, a force opposes its motion
slides.notes: Inside the field both sides cut field lines, but their emfs act in opposite senses around the coil and cancel.

slides.title: Flux and emf against time
bullets: The emf is minus the gradient of the flux graph
Each pulse of emf lasts the time the coil takes to move its own width

slides.title: Timing the pulses
slides.question: A square 100-turn coil of side 5.0 cm moves at a steady 3.0 $\text{cm s}^{-1}$ through a region of uniform field 0.30 T, at right angles to its plane. The region is 12 cm wide. Find (a) the emf while the coil is entering the field and (b) how long the coil is completely inside the field.
slides.hint: While entering, only one side cuts the field. For (b), the coil is fully inside from the moment its back edge enters until its front edge reaches the far side of the region.

steps.text: (a) Only the leading side cuts the field

slides.title: Pulling a coil out of a field
slides.question: A 20-turn square coil of side 10 cm and resistance 2.0 Ω is pulled at a steady 0.40 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ out of a uniform field of 0.50 T at right angles to its plane. Find (a) the induced current and (b) the force needed to pull the coil at constant speed, and (c) show that the power you supply equals the power dissipated in the coil.
slides.hint: Only the side still in the field cuts it, so use $\varepsilon = NBvL$ and Ohm's law. That side carries the current in $N$ turns, so the opposing force is $NBIL$.

steps.text: (a) The side still in the field gives an emf of 0.40 V
(b) The force on that side opposes the motion
Power dissipated in the coil: the same, so energy is conserved

slides.notes: This links Lenz's law to energy: the work done by the pulling force becomes thermal energy in the coil.

points.guide: A uniform magnetic field induces a sinusoidal varying emf in a coil rotating within it.
aims: Explain why a coil rotating at a steady rate in a uniform field produces a sinusoidal emf.
Identify the positions of the coil at which the emf is zero and at which it is greatest.

slides.title: The ac generator
bullets: A coil turns at a steady rate in a uniform field, driven by a turbine or an engine
$B$ and $A$ stay the same, but the angle changes steadily: $\theta = \omega t$
So the flux linkage, $NBA\cos\omega t$, varies like a cosine
The emf is the rate of change of flux linkage, so it varies sinusoidally too: an alternating emf
Slip rings and brushes connect the turning coil to the outside circuit
slides.notes: $\omega = 2\pi f$ comes from circular motion (A.2). A hand-cranked generator joined to an oscilloscope or data logger shows the sine wave.

slides.title: When is the emf zero?
bullets: Plane of the coil at right angles to the field: the flux is greatest but not changing at that instant, so $\varepsilon = 0$
Plane of the coil parallel to the field: the flux is zero but changing fastest, so $\varepsilon$ is greatest
The emf peaks a quarter of a turn after the flux linkage peaks
Think of the sides: the emf is greatest when they cut straight across the field lines

slides.title: Inside an ac generator
slides.alt: A rectangular coil turns about a horizontal axle between an N pole above and an S pole below, with the field B pointing down. The axle carries two slip rings, joined to the two ends of the coil. Two fixed brushes press on the rings and are joined to the circuit.
bullets: The coil turns in the field, driven by a turbine or an engine
Each end of the coil is joined to its own slip ring, which turns with it
Fixed brushes press on the rings and carry the current to the circuit
slides.notes: Drawn at the instant when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so the flux through it is zero.

slides.title: The coil at four positions
slides.alt: The coil seen end-on at the start and after a quarter, a half and three-quarters of a turn, with the field pointing down the page. At the start and after half a turn the coil is at right angles to the field: flux greatest, emf zero. After a quarter and three-quarters of a turn the coil is parallel to the field: flux zero, emf greatest, and the current in each side has reversed between the two.
bullets: Coil at right angles to $B$: $\Phi$ greatest, $\varepsilon = 0$
Coil parallel to $B$: $\Phi = 0$, $\varepsilon$ greatest
The current in each side reverses every half turn
slides.notes: In the end-on views, a dot is current out of the page and a cross is current into it. The blue side carries current out of the page after a quarter turn and into it after three-quarters.

slides.title: Flux linkage and emf against time
bullets: The emf is minus the gradient of the flux-linkage graph
Zero emf where the flux graph is flat; largest emf where it is steepest

slides.title: Generators in power stations
bullets: Steam, water or wind turns a turbine, which turns the generator
Large generators usually turn electromagnets inside fixed coils: only the relative motion matters
Mains electricity is generated at 50 Hz or 60 Hz, so the generators run at a fixed speed
The induced current in the coils feels a force that opposes the rotation, so the turbine must keep doing work
slides.notes: Guide linking question: the efficiency of generating electricity depends on the energy source (B.5 sources, A.3 efficiency).

slides.title: Average emf in a quarter turn
slides.question: A generator coil has 150 turns, each 5.0 cm by 3.0 cm, and turns at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.20 T. Find (a) the greatest flux linkage of the coil and (b) the average emf during the quarter turn from the position of greatest flux to the position of zero flux.
slides.hint: (a) The flux linkage is greatest when the field passes straight through the coil. (b) A quarter turn takes a quarter of the period; use Faraday's law with the change in flux linkage.

steps.text: Average emf over the quarter turn

slides.notes: The peak emf is higher than this average: calculus gives $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega \approx 14$ V. That formula is not in the data booklet and is not needed.

slides.title: Timing the peaks
slides.question: A coil turns steadily at 20 revolutions per second in a uniform field. At $t = 0$ the coil's plane is perpendicular to the field. State the emf at $t = 0$, and find the first time after that at which the emf is greatest.
slides.hint: At which position is the flux not changing at all, and at which is it changing fastest? How far must the coil turn between them?

steps.text: At $t = 0$ the flux is greatest and momentarily not changing
The emf is greatest a quarter turn later, when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field

points.guide: The effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
aims: Explain how changing the frequency of rotation affects the peak emf and the period of the alternating emf.
Describe ways of increasing the emf from a generator.

slides.title: Turning faster
bullets: Double the rotation frequency: the same change in flux happens in half the time
So the rate of change of flux linkage doubles: the peak emf doubles
The period halves, so the frequency of the ac doubles too
The peak emf is proportional to the rotation frequency
slides.notes: The dashed curve on the generator graph shows both effects at once.

slides.title: Increasing a generator's emf
bullets: More turns $N$: more flux linkage to change
A larger coil area $A$
A stronger field $B$, for example from electromagnets
An iron core inside the coil, to strengthen the field through it
Faster rotation, where the frequency of the supply does not have to stay fixed
slides.notes: This answers one of the guiding questions for D.4, on increasing the power output of generators.

slides.title: A bicycle dynamo
slides.question: A bicycle dynamo gives an alternating emf with a peak of 6.0 V when its magnet spins at 20 Hz inside a fixed coil. The cyclist slows down, and the magnet now spins at 15 Hz. Find the new peak emf and the new period of the ac.
slides.hint: The peak emf is proportional to the rotation frequency. For the period, use $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$.

steps.text: Peak emf is proportional to frequency

slides.notes: This is why bicycle lights powered by a dynamo dim when the cyclist slows down. The period was 0.050 s before.

slides.title: Two changes at once
slides.question: A small generator gives a peak emf of 40 V when its coil turns at 60 revolutions per second. It is rebuilt with twice as many turns on the coil, and then turned at 30 revolutions per second in the same field. Find the new peak emf and the new frequency of the ac.
slides.hint: Deal with each change separately: what does doubling the turns do to the emf, and what does halving the rotation frequency do?

steps.text: Twice the turns: twice the flux linkage, so twice the emf
Half the rotation frequency: half the rate of change
The ac frequency equals the rotation frequency
